item.title: ICE Targets ‘Detention Desert’ With New Facility in North Carolina
item.description:
For weeks, residents near the long-dormant Rivers Correctional Institution in Winton, N.C., have noticed trucks inside the prison’s gates, people walking around the entrance and fences being erected.

Internal documents obtained by The New York Times show that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement plans to open a detention center at the complex in northeastern North Carolina by the end of the year. The facility is owned by GEO Group, one of the largest private prison operators in the country. Contract negotiations are ongoing, but the documents show that the facility will have about 1,400 beds, making it among the largest detention centers on the East Coast.

The opening of the facility — the first of its kind in North Carolina — signals that even as ICE has been retreating from its plan to buy up warehouses around the country, it remains determined to increase its capacity for detaining people as part of the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.

Documents obtained by The Times in June show that ICE plans to offload seven warehouses that it bought for more than $700 million, scaling back a signature initiative under the previous homeland security secretary, Kristi Noem. The Department of Homeland Security sent a letter to Pennsylvania officials this month saying that it no longer planned to use a warehouse in Berks County.

But it continues to partner with private companies like GEO Group to repurpose existing prison complexes in places like North Carolina, Colorado and Arizona, all of which have large immigrant populations.

The agency has to find bed space in places that are perceived as “more friendly” toward such facilities and do not prohibit them, said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former ICE official who has served in Republican and Democratic administrations.

At the same time, North Carolina and its surrounding states are a so-called detention desert. Most detainees in the region are often taken to facilities farther south — as happened during the immigration crackdown in Charlotte last year — which costs more time, money and resources. Immigration lawyers and advocates say that a new detention center near the Virginia border could greatly increase agents’ capacity to detain more people across neighboring states.

North Carolina, which has a powerful Republican-controlled legislature, also recently passed laws that require sheriffs and state law enforcement agencies to cooperate with ICE, which is likely to increase the need for capacity.

The Winton facility is poised to make North Carolina a major hub for ICE detentions along the East Coast, said Stefanía Arteaga, the co-founder of Carolina Migrant Network, an immigrant rights group.

The internal documents show that the ICE field office in Washington plans to manage the detention center. A state official, who requested anonymity to discuss private planning, said the facility could be open as soon as late September.

The contract negotiations have not been made public by GEO Group, which did not respond to requests seeking comment. A spokesperson for ICE said in a statement that the agency had “no new detention centers to announce at this time.”

“It should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U.S. and is actively working to expand detention space,” the statement said.

Since President Trump took office in January 2025, federal immigration agents have arrested more than 6,300 people in North Carolina, which is double the number of arrests made during the previous two years combined, according to the Deportation Data Project, an academic group.

In Hertford County, N.C., whose county seat is Winton, some local officials have expressed concerns about being kept in the dark over the federal government’s plans, as they try to manage all the speculation. The county is heavily Democratic.

“This is the most divisive issue that we’ve had in this area,” said Mayor Weyling J. White of Ahoskie, about 10 miles from Winton, noting that he had major reservations about having an ICE-operated facility nearby. “What kind of quality of life do those jobs bring?”

The county, which has a population of less than 20,000, is predominantly Black with pockets of Haitian and Mexican communities. Its poverty rate is about 23 percent, nearly double the statewide rate.

It also sits in a competitive congressional district, currently held by Representative Don Davis, a Democrat. The district was redrawn last year to favor the Republican candidate, Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel. Neither candidate responded to requests for comment on Thursday. Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, also did not respond to a request for comment about the facility.

Well-paying jobs are scarce in the county, so some see the new ICE detention center as an economic lifeline. Others worry about becoming another flashpoint in the immigration crackdown and serving as an outpost for a deeply polarizing federal agency.

The former Rivers Correctional Institution, which closed in 2021 as the Biden administration moved to end federal contracts with for-profit prisons, also has a history of poor conditions.

A federal report of private prisons in 2016 found that Rivers had the highest rates of inmate-on-inmate sexual misconduct, violence, contraband finds (excluding cellphones) and positive drug tests. More recently, prisons across the state have struggled to find employees, and it is unclear how Rivers would fare if it reopened.

“Part of my worry is that we’re not prepared for what’s going to happen when that place opens,” said Jennifer Smyth, who teaches English to nonnative speakers in Hertford County. Even if the county doesn’t see more ICE arrests, she says she worries about increased activity in other parts of the state.

Residents say the financial struggles and need for job creation are evident: Downtown Winton has several abandoned buildings, and the surrounding infrastructure is easily prone to flooding.

But a steel manufacturer is expected to bring more than 700 high-paying jobs to Hertford County by 2030. On GEO Group’s website, there is one job posting for a facility maintenance manager in Rivers; the pay minimum is $72,800.

Leroy Douglas, a Hertford County commissioner who politically identifies as an independent, said the two recent fatal shootings by ICE agents in Texas and Maine had made some residents more resistant to having an immigration detention facility in their backyard. But plenty of others, he added, approve of the plan, especially those who lost their jobs when the Rivers prison closed in 2021.

It is unclear how many locals would be employed there. In 2021, the prison employed about 300 people.

While he doesn’t agree with a lot of ICE’s aggressive tactics, Mr. Douglas said he did not believe that agents would be “running rampant around Hertford County, because that’s not what this is about.”

“If they open up, I really see no negative change in our actual community,” said Mr. Douglas, whose wife worked as a correctional officer at GEO Group decades ago before moving into administrative roles at the company. “I actually see a positive one because there would be a few more jobs.”

Mr. Douglas says he has had no communication with ICE or GEO Group leaders. Other county commissioners did not respond to requests for comment.

In Facebook posts speculating about the prison reopening, comment sections have turned into broader debates about the morality of ICE and border security.

Local activists have begun to mobilize against the facility, organizing protests and flooding county officials with questions. Bobby Ray Riddick, who retired years ago and used to work at a chicken processing plant, is one of them, with 10,000 followers on Facebook.

“This is going to be a ride that I don’t think we’re ready for,” Mr. Riddick said.

item.title: Clint Reilly, Political Consultant Known for Feuding, Dies at 79
item.description:
Clint Reilly, a feared and respected political consultant who ran winning campaigns in California, but whose combustible personality sometimes upstaged the candidates he worked for, died on Saturday in San Francisco. He was 79.

His death was announced by The San Francisco Examiner, which Mr. Reilly bought in 2020, two decades after an only-in-San-Francisco feud with the paper’s management. The cause of death, in a hospital, was chronic lung disease, Frank Holland, a family friend, said.

Mr. Reilly advised some of California’s most successful Democrats of the 1980s and ’90s, including Nancy Pelosi, Dianne Feinstein and Barbara Boxer, whose careers all began in the Bay Area. In 1999, he became a candidate himself, running for mayor of San Francisco and finishing fourth after spending $3.5 million of his own money.

The son of a milkman, Mr. Reilly possessed a granular knowledge of voting blocs and an adman’s instinct for distilling a winning message. He was an early adopter of using computers to identify voters by demographics and interests, so they could be targeted individually. His direct-mail and TV ads delivered a visceral punch, often through attacks on opponents.

“The guy’s a genius,” Richard Riordan, a rare Republican client, told The Los Angeles Times after Mr. Reilly guided him to unexpected victory in the 1993 Los Angeles mayoral race.

As the manager of Ms. Pelosi’s first congressional campaign in 1987, Mr. Reilly coined a prophetic slogan for the future House Speaker: “A voice that will be heard.”

But not all of Mr. Reilly’s clients were pleased with his work. In 1989, after managing two successful mayoral races for Ms. Feinstein, he quit her campaign for governor during the Democratic primary while she was recovering from a hysterectomy. Before telling his client, he faxed reporters the news that he was resigning, saying that she wasn’t working hard enough.

“I am free at last,” Ms. Feinstein responded. She went on to win the primary, lose the general election to Pete Wilson, a Republican, and win a U.S. Senate seat in 1992 — all without Mr. Reilly’s help.

Mr. Reilly goaded candidates to spend lavishly to win, with the not-coincidental side effect that his fees were also lavish. After growing up with little, he favored Italian suits, drove a red Jaguar and lived in a three-story house with a view of the Golden Gate Bridge in the upscale Sea Cliff neighborhood of San Francisco.

When Quentin L. Kopp was a San Francisco supervisor, he hired Mr. Reilly to manage his long-shot 1979 mayoral challenge to Ms. Feinstein, the incumbent. Mr. Reilly made his reputation during that campaign, which forced Ms. Feinstein into a runoff. But during the race, he was arrested and charged with driving drunk.

Mr. Kopp’s supporters urged him to fire Mr. Reilly, he recalled in an interview. He refused, and the two remained friends, though he took to jokingly referring to Mr. Reilly as “Satan,” for his volatile temperament. (Mr. Reilly said that he quit drinking soon after the arrest.)

At a holiday party at Mr. Reilly’s home some years later, Mr. Kopp said, “Clint’s mother implored me to stop referring to him as Satan,” which he did.

Mr. Reilly’s purchase of The Examiner followed a long saga in and out of courtrooms, starting in 1993, when he visited the office of the executive editor, Phil Bronstein, to complain about the paper’s coverage of a client and left in an ambulance with a broken ankle.

He sued Mr. Bronstein, claiming that the editor had shoved him; he also sued the newspaper’s publisher, William Randolph Hearst III, who was present during the incident. Mr. Reilly won an undisclosed settlement, and The Examiner expressed regret for his injury.

In 2000, Mr. Reilly was back in court with The Examiner, this time suing its owner, the Hearst Corporation, on antitrust grounds to stop it from buying the rival San Francisco Chronicle.

Lawyers for The Examiner called the suit an attempt to settle old scores, after the newspaper had backed Mayor Willie L. Brown Jr. the previous year during Mr. Reilly’s failed mayoral campaign. A federal judge ruled in favor of Hearst.

Two decades later, after The Examiner had passed through several different owners, Mr. Reilly acquired the newspaper and a sister publication, SF Weekly, for an undisclosed sum. He reinvented The Examiner as a broadsheet that published three days a week, with an accompanying digital site, focused on local news.

After Mr. Reilly left political consulting in 1995, he became a successful commercial real estate investor, starting with his purchase that year of the Merchants Exchange Building downtown for $18 million. He also owned event spaces and hospitality businesses.

Clinton Thomas Reilly was born on Jan. 13, 1947, in Oakland, Calif., the eldest of 10 children of Joe Reilly, who delivered milk for Berkeley Farms, and Bess (Stone) Reilly, who operated a concessions stand at the Oakland Coliseum. He grew up in San Leandro, a working-class city in the East Bay.

At 14, he declared his intention to become a Roman Catholic priest and entered St. Patrick’s Seminary in Menlo Park, earning a bachelor’s degree in philosophy. But after nine years of study, he abandoned his plans, concluding that social justice could be better pursued through politics.

“I think initially, intuitively, I wanted to get involved in politics because that was a place where you could improve people’s lives and make the biggest impact on the direction of the world,” he told The Los Angeles Times in 1994.

His first client was one of his former seminary professors, the Rev. Eugene J. Boyle, a liberal activist who ran unsuccessfully for State Assembly in 1974.

Mr. Reilly married Janet Koewler, a former aide to Mr. Riordan, in 1995. The two met while he was running the Riordan campaign. She survives him, along with two daughters, Jill and Ava Reilly; six brothers, Kevin, Mark, Brian, Joseph, Matthew and Dan; and a sister, Linette Hamil.

Candidates “are not hiring me because they want me to get along with everybody,” Mr. Reilly once told The Los Angeles Times. “The campaign is a war, you know?”

item.title: Tugboat Captain Pleads Guilty in Miami Crash That Killed 3 Children
item.description:
The captain of a 25-foot tugboat that was pushing a barge when it slammed into a sailboat last year in Miami Beach, killing three children from a sailing camp, pleaded guilty on Tuesday to a count of seaman’s manslaughter.

The captain, Yusiel Lopez Insua, 47, of Miami, admitted in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida that his actions caused the collision, according to court documents. He faces up to 10 years in prison.

Prosecutors said Mr. Insua was pushing a barge across Biscayne Bay just before 11:30 a.m. on July 28, 2025, when it struck a stalled sailboat carrying five girls, ages 7 to 13, and a 19-year-old camp counselor. The Miami Yacht Club said the children and the counselor were from a sailing camp run by the Miami Youth Sailing Foundation.

The U.S. Coast Guard received a report that a barge had struck the sailboat near Hibiscus and Monument islands in Miami Beach.

Three of the girls were killed. The Miami-Dade County Medical Examiner’s Office identified two of them as Mila Yankelevich, 7, and Erin Ko, 13. Days later, the family of a third victim, Arielle Buchman, 10, announced that she, too, had died.

Federal prosecutors said that the camp counselor had tried to alert Mr. Insua to the sailboat’s presence, but that his forward view was blocked by part of the tugboat’s structure.

“Three children lost their lives in a tragedy that never should have happened,” Jason A. Reding Quiñones, U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, said in a statement.

Mr. Insua’s lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: Kagan Says Supreme Court Has Stood Up to Trump in Key Cases
item.description:
One of the Supreme Court’s three liberal justices defended her conservative colleagues on Thursday, insisting the court has not been too deferential to President Trump.

“I think that is a bad rap,” Justice Elena Kagan said during an appearance in Washington State, at an annual gathering of judges and lawyers who work in the judiciary’s Ninth Circuit.

“Is this court very conservative?” she continued. “Does it do a bunch of things that are out of the playbook of the conservative legal movement that I think are deeply wrong? Yes.”

“But,” she added, “is this court kind of a puppet for the current administration? I think definitely not.”

Justice Kagan made the comments as she answered questions posed by an appeals court judge and a lawyer in front of dozens of attendees who work in the nine-state Western region served by the circuit.

Polls have shown declining trust in the institution, and a number of the justices have used recent public appearances to try to defuse the notion that they have become political actors.

Since Mr. Trump returned to office, the court has signed off on a series of his policies on a temporary basis, through emergency orders that have allowed the administration to carry out many of its executive orders even while their legality was being weighed in court.

But Justice Kagan, when asked how she viewed criticism of the court for greenlighting the administration policies, insisted the reality of the court’s record is more nuanced.

In its most recent term, which ended in late June, the Supreme Court cleared the way for a number of long-term conservative goals, she noted. She cited decisions to allow the president sweeping power to fire leaders of independent agencies and to significantly weaken the Voting Rights Act of 1965, a key civil rights law.

But several times, Justice Kagan continued, a majority of the justices joined together to reject Mr. Trump’s initiatives. The justices agreed to invalidate his sweeping emergency tariffs, to strike down his executive order ending birthright citizenship for the children of undocumented immigrants and some temporary foreign visitors and to nix his attempt to fire a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors.

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

“I don’t see this as a court that is just going to rubber-stamp what the current administration does — quite the opposite,” she said.

Justice Kagan was in the majority in each of those cases, joined by the court’s other two liberal justices but also several justices appointed by Republican presidents. The court’s decisions rejecting those policies infuriated the president.

Mr. Trump lashed out at the justices who rejected his tariffs program, including two justices nominated by him, calling them “fools and lap dogs.”

When Justice Kagan addressed the same conference last year, she used the appearance to express concern about how the court handled a barrage of emergency applications on Trump administration policies.

At the start of Mr. Trump’s second term, he issued a series of executive orders, many of which faced immediate court challenges that quickly arrived at the court on the emergency docket. Applications on that docket, often referred to by critics as the shadow docket, typically come to the justices without full briefing or a robust lower court record, and the justices sometimes rule on applications without explaining their reasoning.

The court, she said then, should “be cautious about acting on the emergency docket.”

At Thursday’s event, Justice Kagan said that she thought the court had “made some improvements” in the past year in how it has handled emergency requests. For instance, she said she believed that the court’s “transparency has become better by a fair bit” because the court has issued more orders that included some reasoning.

Still, she said she believed the court has still been “granting too many of these applications,” creating a “kind of momentum” that has led to the filing of more emergency requests.

The justice’s comments were her first public statements since she testified to Congress earlier this month to ask for millions more dollars in funding for security for the justices. She was joined on Capitol Hill by Justice Amy Coney Barrett, a conservative justice nominated by Mr. Trump, to describe the rising number of threats made against the justices.

On Thursday, she told attendees of the judicial conference that life for a Supreme Court justice has changed since she was appointed to the court in 2010 by President Barack Obama and the justices faced fewer threats.

“I drove myself to work, went out grocery shopping, went to the movies,” she said of her early years on the court. “I did the normal things that people do without any security in sight. I felt like, you know, just like a normal everyday person. And that’s not true for us anymore.”

item.title: The Roller Skater Trying to Reframe the History of Farmworker Rights
item.description:
It was Magic Monday, the weekly convocation of roller skaters on Venice Beach in Los Angeles, and a nearly sacred observance for Johnny Itliong. As usual, he was helping out his entrepreneurial friends on the boardwalk by sporting their merch — a “Skate Famous” branded hat from one, stickers on his gear from others.

The music was bumping and the sun had come out. On most Magic Mondays, that and a little weed would have been all Itliong needed. But on this afternoon, as he felt his way through the steps of a line dance and passed a vape to a buddy, he had more on his mind.

Days before, the news that Cesar Chavez had been accused of sexually abusing girls landed like a bomb, forcing a reckoning over one of the nation’s few Latino civil rights icons.

Those girls were the daughters of farmworker organizers whose movement Chavez had famously led. Itliong, 61, felt sorrow for the victims, who included the sister of a close friend. But the revelation also brought something like vindication — and opportunity.

Itliong’s father was Larry Itliong, the Filipino American farmworker leader who was perennially overshadowed by the younger and more telegenic Chavez. While Chavez’s name was reverently bestowed on schools, streets and libraries, the Itliong name remained largely unknown even in Delano, the agricultural town in California’s Central Valley where Johnny was born and Larry died.

For decades, the son has made it his life’s work to change this. He has traveled California, attending United Farm Workers events and ceremonies honoring the farm labor movement to proclaim what he sees as the truth: After his father spent decades toiling in the fields, learning multiple languages to communicate better with workers and making grueling treks to find them, he said, Chavez and his followers muscled in on their work and took the credit.

“I have been fighting to get the story of my father out for decades and have been waiting for the U.F.W. to step up and honor Larry as they do Cesar,” he said at one such event.

His efforts, he said, have cost him money, untold time, three marriages and his relationships with his three children.

But now the world could find out what Itliong had believed for as long as he could remember.

“He was a narcissist,” Itliong told me, jabbing his two middle fingers into the air whenever he said Chavez’s name. He paused to nod at friends passing by on their skates.

“They’re writing about my dad!” he told them.

He was confident and breezy, joking and laughing as he glided around the rink. But later, he reflected on a life in which he has often felt thwarted — punished, even — for trying to carry forward his family’s legacy.

“I want this for my children,” he said. “I may be a piece of shit, but I want them to be proud of their grandfather.”

Everyone was waiting for Itliong, and when he finally appeared on the video call, he apologized; he had been looking for a place to plug in his laptop.

In the weeks since the Chavez news had broken, he had given about two dozen interviews reminding journalists that the movement Chavez had come to embody was actually about much more than a single person. He told The Los Angeles Times that his father’s purpose “was to raise everybody up.”

Members of a loosely organized group of Asian American civil rights advocates had read the coverage. Seeing an opportunity to highlight the work of Filipino American leaders, they asked Itliong to help them strategize.

“This is a very critical moment with this openness,” said Eric Chen, a pastor. He began working as an activist after a mass shooting at a ballroom that left 11 mostly older Asian Americans dead and devastated the Asian American enclave in Los Angeles County that he calls home. “We’ve got to strike while the iron is hot.”

The question was how. Chen and Itliong had identified a turning point, but they had a harder time figuring out a mission. All they knew was that they wanted to bring more attention to Larry Itliong’s contributions without deifying him or anyone else. In the end, they decided that they would host a kind of informational “round table” and news conference, both aimed at moving the celebration of the farmworker movement from Chavez’s birthday to some other day and elevating the stories of others in the movement.

Chen offered a benediction.

“I pray that as we embark on this journey to rewrite history, that it would be a journey of healing as well, a journey of redemption,” he said as the others nodded solemnly in their little boxes on the screen. “Because, Lord, we know that it was not about one man. It was a movement.”

Larry Itliong married six times, and Johnny’s mother was mostly absent from his childhood. He was cared for by a large, shifting group of aunts and uncles, related by blood and not, who were animated by the common goal of building a farmworker movement.

In his first memories, he is a toddler watching Mickey Mouse cartoons on a jet to the Philippines with one such couple — a Filipino American doctor and his wife. They took him to visit the rice paddies his father left behind when he came to the United States in 1929.

Larry Itliong had begun rallying agricultural workers up and down the West Coast in the 1930s, from the canneries of Alaska to the vegetable fields of the Coachella Valley. He spent decades pushing for higher pay and safer working conditions for farmworkers who were then, as now, nearly all immigrants.

As the leader of the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee, he helped orchestrate the Delano, Calif., grape strike and boycott of 1965.

Historians say it was only after Larry Itliong helped persuade the predominantly Mexican and Mexican American leaders of the nascent National Farm Workers Association to join the Filipinos’ strike that the modern farm labor movement was born.

Growing up in Delano in the 1960s and ’70s, Johnny sometimes rose in the early hours of the morning to follow older relatives into the grapevines, where they did the backbreaking work it took to feed the nation.

Even as a child, he had a sense that his family was at the center of something important. After dinner, he and the other children would stay outside while the adults talked inside Delano’s Filipino Hall, their voices often erupting into shouts. In conversation, Itliong routinely rattles off names of other leaders who he says were harmed by the cult of personality surrounding Chavez. Many of these organizers, like his father, understood the sacrifices that it took to make it as a farm laborer. Itliong said he could relate to this struggle in a way that Chavez’s children could not.

But during those years, forces beyond Larry’s control were conspiring to change the course of history.

One of the founders of the National Farm Workers Association was Chavez. At the time, he was a young man amassing followers as he sought to transform the long effort to unionize migrant farmworkers into a broader civil rights movement.

Born on an Arizona farm just two years before Larry Itliong arrived on the West Coast, Chavez was a sharp strategist and strong-willed Mexican American leader who galvanized Latinos, a fast-growing demographic in search of their own Martin Luther King Jr.

In Itliong’s telling, Chavez’s growing fame created an opening for his ambitious cohort to elbow his father and other longtime organizers out of the way. The tension between Chavez’s mostly Latino followers and the Filipino Americans close to Itliong lingers even now.

Itliong remembered his father’s anger when Chavez moved the United Farm Workers’ headquarters from Delano to an isolated community in the Tehachapi Mountains, farther from farmworkers’ homes. He remembered how journalists and documentarians focused on Chavez and did not widen the frame to include Larry or other Filipinos.

“Their passion is a product of their frustration,” said Matt Garcia, a historian at Dartmouth College and a Chavez biographer who has written critically about the way Chavez wielded his power. “And that frustration is legit.”

While Professor Garcia said there was no evidence of a conspiracy by Chavez and his allies to exclude Larry Itliong or other Filipinos from the history books, he said that Itliong and Chavez represented clashing visions of the farmworker movement.

Larry was a strident “meat and potatoes” union organizer, eager to flex the untapped power of farmworkers like himself. Chavez, as a Mexican American, was a member of a demographic majority of farmworkers, and he saw the movement as a broader social one. Collective bargaining and the fine points of contracts, Professor Garcia said, didn’t interest him.

Chavez also had “a will to power,” Professor Garcia said, and it was fulfilled by society’s impulse to venerate individuals instead of the messy collectives who make change. And so Chavez became the face of the movement.

The United Farm Workers union he left behind had been grappling with his legacy since long before the revelations of abuse. In response to questions from The New York Times, the group acknowledged that there were “many, many names who don’t have enough recognition,” including but not limited to Itliong.

“The best way the modern U.F.W. can honor Larry Itliong’s legacy is to continue what he spent his incredible life doing,” the statement said: “organizing workers to win the dignity and protections of a union contract.”

The Chavez family declined to comment for this article.

Much of the maneuvering that ultimately sidelined Larry Itliong took place when his son Johnny was too young to understand what was happening. In 1971, Larry resigned from the union that became the United Farm Workers. His children helped care for him as he suffered from A.L.S., the harrowing degenerative disease, until his death in 1977.

“I just remember the doctor sitting in the white chair we had, or yellow leather, or something,” Itliong told me, wiping away tears. “And then the preacher came.”

At age 14, he left home, where life had become turbulent, and stayed with friends or in a car. With the help of an empathetic teacher, he graduated from high school in Delano and moved to the nearest big city, Bakersfield.

He said he worked as a contractor overseas in roles he maintains he can’t talk about. He worked as a chef. He lived in the San Francisco Bay Area and in Nevada, where the last of his marriages dissolved in acrimony.

He is estranged from his children — not by his choice, he said, though according to divorce court records, he has not taken opportunities to see them.

In 2004 he was convicted of domestic violence, after an incident in which his wife at the time, Kelly Cornell, said he slapped her and assaulted her while she was on the toilet. Itliong maintains he was not violent and said Cornell lied. More than two decades later, Cornell said she harbors no “hard feelings.” But after going for years without child support for their son, now an adult and also named Larry, she said, “I just wish his dad would step up a little bit.”

Reached by text message, the younger Larry, 25, said he didn’t want to talk about his father. He didn’t reply when asked if he felt any connection to his grandfather’s legacy.

On and off for about three decades, Itliong has lived in Los Angeles, mostly hanging around the beach. For money, he said, he helps mount televisions for wealthy customers. A skateboarder for decades, he has also taken up roller skating, joining an enthusiastic community that blasts music and wears glowing lights. He describes his living situation as mobile; he has eschewed many of his possessions to live “the way the manongs lived,” referring to Filipino immigrants like his father.

But when anyone — the office of an elected official, a Filipino American nonprofit, a reporter — calls asking to talk about his dad, he picks up. And after the accusations of sexual abuse by Chavez emerged, there were lots of calls.

In Delano as in other communities in the Central Valley, suburban neighborhoods have replaced some of the fields. Still, small reminders of Larry Itliong’s legacy are tucked throughout the town. On Memorial Day weekend, a crowd of siblings, cousins and in-laws held an impromptu gathering at Larry Itliong Unity Park, which was dedicated two years ago. Johnny Itliong had come to spend time with his sister, Sandra Itliong Bowman, who had driven down from the Seattle area.

Sandra’s adult children say that they remember being dismissed by classmates and teachers, even in Delano, when they talked about their grandfather as a historic figure of note. Sandra said she was grateful that her brother had continued to publicize their father’s accomplishments. She wants her seven grandchildren to know where they came from.

“I’m not here to judge anybody,” she said, reluctant to blame anyone for overlooking Larry. “I can only build on the future for the ones who will carry on the legacy.”

The next stop was an elementary school where Itliong’s half sister, Patricia Itliong Serda, worked for decades as a librarian. On the exterior wall of the library, a colorful mural depicts Larry’s journey from the Philippines, the Delano grape strike and symbols of his legacy. Johnny stopped to point out details, including an image of Patricia as a child standing at Larry’s knee as he reads from an open book. Patricia said she worked for years to secure a nonprofit grant to commission the piece.

Most of the students at the school are Filipino American, Latino or a combination of the two, and she said she had poured her energy into teaching them about their heritage. The mural has invited discussion.

“Coming from our little town, it means a lot,” she said. “This is where I can make the most impact.”

Later, Itliong stopped by the cemetery where his father was buried beneath a simple headstone. Itliong once worked there, helping to maintain the grounds.

“I’ve come here at times throughout the years, you know?” he said, almost to himself, as he plucked stray weeds and bits of trash from the grass. Not for the first time in our conversations, Itliong alluded to a sense that his own life hadn’t worked out entirely as he might have hoped.

“Struggling, because my life — you know, I get great satisfaction from helping people, right? But you know the old saying: No good deeds ever go unpunished.”

He said he talked to his father when he visited the grave but never told him about the work he was doing on his behalf. Accolades wouldn’t have interested Larry, Itliong said. He said he used to skip ceremonies and events himself until one day a friend helped him think of things another way.

“‘You’re the connection to him,’” Itliong recalled her saying. “All this weight on the shoulder? It increased a hundredfold. I’m like, ‘Are you kidding me?’”

Soon Itliong was back in Los Angeles, hosting a panel with other Asian American activists. He took his place at the center of a table facing a group of nonprofit workers and labor rights advocates at the Pilipino Workers Center, a nonprofit in Historic Filipinotown.

Itliong was joined on the panel by his longtime friend Desirée Rojas, a daughter of Al Rojas, a farmworker and labor organizer. Rojas’s sister Debra was among the women who upended Chavez’s legacy when they described how he had abused them as young teenage girls.

Itliong seemed nervous, getting up briefly to fiddle with the audiovisual setup. But as others on the makeshift dais spoke about his father’s work, he relaxed into his role as a kind of magnanimous convener.

“It’s always been an honor to be the son of Larry Itliong. Those are very, very hard shoes to step into,” he told the room. “But I’m here now. I’ve been here my whole life, doing exactly what he did, standing up for those who needed to be heard.”

Aquilina Soriano, the director of the Pilipino Workers Center, urged the audience not to let their stories or perspectives remain in that room.

Tell your leaders, she said, that it’s important to pick a different day to celebrate the farm workers’ movement, that it’s important not to simply swap in the name of another imperfect person on every street sign or school that now reads “Cesar Chavez.”

“This is a call to action,” she said. “We still have a lot of work to do.”

To end the day, Itliong invited the audience to join him in what has become known as the unity clap, which begins with a slow clap and builds to the cacophony of loud applause. The Filipino version is punctuated with a cry of “isang baksak,” which roughly translates from Tagalog to “one down” — another day completed, another task done.

“Yeah! Isang baksak!” Itliong yelled, pumping his fists as the applause rang out.

Another task done, many more left. In the days after, Itliong would meet with the others to discuss strategy as Los Angeles County officials debated how to rename things named after Cesar Chavez.

But first, he went skating.

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Democrats Prepare for Possible Election Clashes With Federal Government
item.description:
Democratic state officials are ramping up their preparations to protect against what they view as a new threat to election security: the federal government.

At a meeting in Milwaukee in May, staff members from the offices of every Democratic attorney general and about a dozen Democratic secretaries of state held tabletop exercises to prepare for hypothetical scenarios in the November midterm elections.

In those “war rooms,” said Nick Brown, the Democratic attorney general of the state of Washington, state officials discussed how they would handle a variety of scenarios. What might happen if the F.B.I. showed up, demanding election materials or equipment? What if federal troops or agents were deployed in the country in ways that could intimidate voters or disrupt the election? What if President Trump tried to declare an election-related national emergency?

“The sad reality now is that the federal government is our biggest concern,” Mr. Brown said, adding, “It used to be that the Department of Justice was our No. 1 partner, helping states prepare for election-related issues.”

The Trump administration has not explicitly threatened to make any such moves, and a White House spokeswoman dismissed the Democratic efforts, arguing that the party should instead focus on passing tighter voting laws.

But Mr. Trump, who tried to overturn the results of the 2020 election, told The New York Times this year that he regretted not seizing voting machines after that contest. In his second term, he has appeared increasingly eager to use the federal government’s investigative, prosecutorial and legislative powers to influence how elections are run. His prime-time speech to the nation last week, fanning false claims of election fraud, raised new concerns about possible federal interference in the midterms.

This week, Mr. Trump and his allies seized on reports that roughly 400 noncitizens had cast ballots in New Jersey, after about 6,600 residents had been improperly registered to vote because of a 2023 software error at the Motor Vehicle Commission. (The state’s Democratic governor said what happened was “unacceptable.”)

But Mr. Trump has recently made much broader claims, which remain unsubstantiated, about hundreds of thousands of noncitizens voting illegally in four states. A letter from the Homeland Security Department, sent to one of the states and obtained by The New York Times, indicated that the data cited by Mr. Trump was an initial estimate and was probably highly inflated.

The election security meeting in May was part of a broader effort among Democratic secretaries of state and attorneys general to increase their coordination across the country ahead of the midterm elections.

They are creating two groups to formalize these partnerships: the AGSOS Election Protection PAC, which will work to raise money and elect Democrats to each office, and AGSOS Election Protection Action, a policy arm. The effort is an outgrowth of the existing campaign arms for the national groups representing each office, the Democratic Association of Secretaries of State and the Democratic Attorneys General Association.

“By formalizing this partnership between attorneys general and secretaries of state, we have created a high-functioning hub where other organizations can coordinate actions to protect election results up and down the ballot,” said Sean Rankin, the president of the Democratic Attorneys General Association.

While the holders of the two offices often work closely together in a single state, a top election official in one state will rarely work with an attorney general from another. Democrats say that creating a national network of these two offices is necessary given Mr. Trump’s actions.

“We will use all the tools at our disposal to fight Donald Trump and protect our voting rights,” Cisco Aguilar, the Nevada secretary of state and the chair of the Democratic Association of Secretaries of State, said in a statement.

Abigail Jackson, a White House spokeswoman, suggested that Democrats should be trying to pass the SAVE America Act, a stalled bill of voting restrictions that Mr. Trump has called his top priority.

“If Democrats really cared about securing our elections, they would pass the SAVE America Act, which includes common-sense election integrity measures supported by the vast majority of Americans,” Ms. Jackson said in a statement. Those provisions include requiring a documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote, as well as strict new photo identification requirements. Many eligible voters would not be able to meet the new requirements.

Democrats have pushed back in other ways against Mr. Trump’s election moves. Democratic-led states have refused to hand over private, unredacted voter files to the Justice Department, prompting 30 lawsuits from the administration.

Democratic attorneys general were also behind litigation to block both of the president’s executive orders aimed at changing American election laws. And Democratic secretaries of state have worked to re-create federal election security programs that have been cut by the Trump administration.

But the bellicose language regarding elections from the president and his allies has Democratic state officials on high alert.

Two years ago, Mr. Brown said, efforts to “delay, disrupt, interfere” with an election “would have seemed like a joke.” Now, he added, they “are very real.”

item.title: Black Parents Are Rattled by Mississippi Teen’s Death Among White Friends
item.description:
LaTonya Davis has been following the death of Nolan Wells “constantly on TikTok,” she said, and has been thinking of her 21-year-old nephew, Jayden Holmes, whom she has called her “neph-son” since she took legal guardianship of him when he was 11, after his parents’ deaths.

The death of Mr. Wells, a Black 18-year-old community college athlete from Ocean Springs, Miss., who took a boat to a Mississippi barrier island with white friends on July 4 and did not return, has drawn huge attention on social media and beyond. It has also stoked outrage and deep anxiety among parents like Ms. Davis, who say they have long nursed fears about how their Black children are faring in predominately white environments.

“It was like I was watching one of the things that I’ve always been worried about,” said Ms. Davis, 58, who moved Mr. Holmes from Orlando, Fla., to Miami Beach to raise him.

Local authorities in Mississippi say they believe the death was an accidental drowning. The Jackson County Sheriff’s Department released a statement on July 6 — the day Mr. Wells’s body was found — stating that “no foul play was suspected.” The police have said they believe Mr. Wells at one point left his friends to join another group, and possibly boarded another boat. So far nothing concrete has emerged to contradict that.

Even so, internet sleuths and Black activists have parsed details of the investigation that they say suggest malfeasance. And many Black parents say they see a double standard in the way the case has been handled. The authorities, they say, would not have dismissed the possibility of foul play so quickly had a white youth died at a predominantly Black party.

In that case, “those young Black men” would have been “interrogated to the full extent of the law,” Benjamin L. Crump, a civil rights lawyer representing Mr. Wells’s family, asserted at a news conference this week.

Despite any official suggestion of wrongdoing, the intense scrutiny online has often cast suspicion on the group of Mr. Wells’s friends who went with him to the island. The commentary has at times veered into conspiracy theory and misinformation that has set off its own burst of outrage on behalf of Mr. Wells’s friends.

But the attention has also provided a megaphone for Black social media users to describe their own experiences and fears. They have recalled painful moments as the only Black children in predominately white prep schools, neighborhoods and social settings.

Ashley Stoney, a Black freelance journalist, wrote in New York magazine of group chats lighting up with anxiety over Mr. Wells’s death.

“We talked about how isolating it can feel to be the only Black person and how dangerous it can be if no one truly values your humanity,” she wrote. “What kinds of experiences do our kids have when we aren’t around? Who will protect us when no one is looking?”

The worry is rooted in the long, violent history of racial segregation in America and what integration and assimilation look like in modern society. Some social media users have implied that Black parents shouldn’t allow their children to be the only one in “white spaces.”

That is not always possible “for things that you want to expose them to, depending on where you are,” said Tangala Hollis-Palmer, a mother and lawyer in Grenada, Miss., who is Black.

When she learned about Mr. Wells’s death, her thoughts turned to her children, who navigate similar all-white environments in the Deep South. She doesn’t tell her son, who was the only Black child on his baseball team, to be suspicious of white people, but she does say he must “be aware” of potential mistreatment “because you’re the only one there,” she said.

The worries are not just over physical harm but also social alienation, unintentional or not. Ms. Hollis-Palmer said she paused when her daughter wanted to compete on a dance team that required her to straighten her hair, afraid that it would send the message that she wasn’t good enough. But she acquiesced.

“Your hair is just as beautiful,” she recalled telling her daughter.

The death has also provoked a conversation among Black parents about race, privilege and why they feel their children have a more difficult time receiving justice.

Mr. Wells’s family has been castigated even for questioning the initial reports of their son’s death, Nolan’s mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, said. Some members of the public have been baffled by the Black response.

“Any parent that would be in this situation, you would do anything to find out what happened to your child.” she said.

Mississippi’s history of racial violence and denied justice is also factoring into the skepticism. Last September, a 21-year-old Black student named Demartravion “Trey” Reed was found dead, hanging from a tree on the campus of a small college in northwest Mississippi. The death was ruled a suicide, and no evidence has emerged to suggest otherwise, but Mr. Crump is representing Mr. Reed’s family and has commissioned an independent autopsy in the Reed case. The report has not yet been released.

Then there’s the case of Damien Cameron, a 29-year-old Black man whose face was bloody and swollen when his body arrived at the Mississippi State Medical Examiner’s Office in August 2021 after an altercation with sheriff’s deputies. His cause of death was ruled undetermined, but three pathologists who examined Mr. Cameron’s autopsy report at the request of The New York Times and Mississippi Today said his death should have been ruled a homicide. The same state medical examiner is also conducting Mr. Wells’s autopsy.

The circumstances of Mr. Wells’s death have resonated beyond the particulars of Mississippi and its history as Black families navigate the white worlds of a more integrated America.

Mr. Holmes, Ms. Davis’s nephew, has found himself in situations where, like Mr. Wells, he was the only Black person.

“It’s not necessarily something that I’m nervous about,” he said. “But it is something that is always top of mind. I always assume that I’m being judged.”

Ms. Davis’s worries have gone beyond judgment to fear.

“Anytime the phone rings, late at night, if he’s out with his friends, my heart just drops,” Ms. Davis said.

item.title: How a Grieving Trump Decided to Back Lindsey Graham’s Sister for Senate
item.description:
The morning after Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina died, President Trump floated his choice for serving the remainder of his term: a little-known House member he saw as a loyal MAGA foot soldier.

The president had been fond of that House member, Russell Fry, ever since he had defeated a congressman who had voted to impeach him. Mr. Trump relayed the idea to Gov. Henry McMaster, who held the power to appoint an interim senator, on a call that Sunday morning, according to three people familiar with the conversation.

Mr. McMaster had another name in mind: Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister and an advocate for disability rights in a suburb of Columbia, S.C. Nobody seemed to know very much about her.

The exchange between Mr. Trump and Mr. McMaster kick-started one of the most high-stakes weeks in South Carolina’s political history, one that has shaped its first open Republican primary election for a Senate seat in more than two decades. The scramble culminated when Mr. Trump gave Ms. Graham his blessing — not only as a short-term caretaker for her late brother’s seat, but for the highly coveted six-year term.

The account of how Mr. Trump decided to back Ms. Graham is based on interviews with 10 people familiar with the events leading to Mr. Trump’s decision. It captures a tumultuous stretch for Mr. McMaster, who found himself fielding calls from a veterinary emergency room, and a fraught week for the president, whom several people described as uncharacteristically emotional about the death of his friend.

“It’s mind boggling,” said Kevin Bishop, who served as Mr. Graham’s communications director for 27 years. “The grieving, the campaigning, the funeral procession — and by the way, there’s an election two weeks after that, too.”

Mr. Trump’s selection of a political unknown is a significant gamble at a critical moment when control of both chambers is at stake.

Polls conducted last week showed Representative Ralph Norman, a member of the House Freedom Caucus, leading the entire field. Mr. Fry, who is also running, is widely considered to be a contender, too, as is Mark Sanford, the former South Carolina governor and congressman whose political career was marred by a high-profile affair. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, is the Democratic nominee for the seat in the solidly red state.

If no candidate receives a majority of votes on Aug. 11, a runoff would take place two weeks later.

Mr. McMaster, who was the first statewide elected official to endorse Mr. Trump in 2016, spent the night after he learned of Mr. Graham’s death surrounded by his staff at the governor’s mansion. First, they got the word of his death out to Mr. Graham’s extended political network. Then they pivoted to conversations about who should replace him.

By the morning, Mr. McMaster had made up his mind.

“The governor had come to the conclusion that Darline would be the perfect caretaker,” said a person familiar with his thinking. “It so fit with the narrative of Lindsey Graham.”

The siblings had formed a particularly tight bond after losing both of their parents in a 15-month stretch when Mr. Graham was 22 years old and his sister was 13. Mr. Graham later became his sister’s legal guardian.

Mr. McMaster called the president on Sunday morning. Mr. Trump raised the idea of giving the temporary post to Mr. Fry, 41, who had proven his loyalty to the president by defeating Tom Rice, one of 10 House Republicans who had voted to impeach the president over his role in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

Mr. McMaster suggested Ms. Graham, discussing the closeness of her relationship with the late senator. The president said he thought it was a great idea, the three people said.

Then the governor called Ms. Graham, who agreed through tears to finish her brother’s term. There were no conversations about replacing him permanently, three people familiar with the conversation said.

Shortly after that call, Mr. McMaster’s beloved bulldog Mac fell ill from exhaustion. He continued to field calls about Mr. Graham’s seat from a veterinary hospital.

At that moment, Mr. Trump and the White House staff appeared to still have Mr. Fry in mind for the primary election. The president and the congressman were engaged in conversation over text messages, one person familiar with the exchange said. Mr. Trump made an appearance on Newsmax, calling Mr. Fry “outstanding” and saying he “could see” him succeeding his late friend.

But concerns were bubbling up about Mr. Fry’s candidacy — namely that he could create a critical vacancy in the House if he won the seat in the Senate. A special election wouldn’t occur before early 2027, leaving Republicans with one less vote at the start of a new Congress.

The White House press team, asked to comment on the events of the week after Mr. Graham’s death, pointed to Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt’s comments during Thursday’s press briefing, when she said the president had concluded that Ms. Graham would “carry on her brother’s legacy of public service in that beautiful state.”

Around the same time, Ms. Graham met with the president in the Oval Office, flanked by Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the chief of staff, Susie Wiles, among others.

The morning meeting started with the country’s most powerful people sharing stories about Mr. Graham. Mr. Trump, who is not known to show emotion, appeared upset by the loss, two people said.

Then his aides handed him a list of names to succeed the late senator. It included Trey Gowdy, the former congressman and Fox News host who had already told multiple people he did not want the job, and Mr. Norman, who had endorsed Nikki Haley for president in 2024, and whom Mr. Trump quickly dismissed. It also included Mr. Fry, whom the president praised. Ms. Graham was on the list.

She spoke up, two people said, and asked the president what he thought about her running for the seat.

The idea had occurred to her earlier that week, after multiple people — from close friends to nationally known politicians — had reached out and encouraged her to start a formal bid, three people said.

Ms. Graham, 62, is widely respected for her work helping people with disabilities find jobs, most recently as commissioner of a state agency for blind residents. Some close to Mr. Graham felt her candidacy would best reflect his desires.

Mr. Trump appeared to be taken with the idea. He was also impressed by her composure, two people said. He told the room that he hated some people on the list, liked other people on the list, but loved only one candidate, and that was Ms. Graham, two people said.

He publicly endorsed her the next day.

But the work to transform a private, grieving sister into a candidate for the Senate was just beginning.

Ms. Graham, 62, became South Carolina’s first female senator when she was sworn in last week to serve out her brother’s term. In South Carolina, few people appeared to know anything about her politics or her identity beyond her close ties to Mr. Graham.

Even in her own neighborhood and the nearby capital, Columbia, residents said she was not often seen about town. Ms. Graham sat for an interview with the Fox News host Sean Hannity on Monday, but by Friday, she had not agreed to participate in any future debates with other candidates. Her staff declined to make her available for an interview for this story.

Advocates who have worked with Ms. Graham describe her as a skilled relationship-builder who has made a significant impact for people with disabilities.

“People have nothing but nice things to say about her, and that’s not always the case, especially when politics is involved,” said Kimberly Tissot, president and C.E.O. of Able SC, an organization that advocates for people with disabilities.

Katrina Shealy, 71, described herself as a close friend of Ms. Graham’s. She is one of five former state senators who were defeated three years ago after they blocked a near-total abortion ban in the state. But she said politics had rarely, if ever, come up with Ms. Graham — and certainly not the issue of abortion. Instead, they liked to drink wine on her back porch, watch Ms. Shealy’s pet donkeys and talk about their faith and families.

Ms. Graham is deeply religious and a mother of two grown daughters. Multiple friends described her as focused on her family.

“Her mannerism is not to get involved with politics that way,” Ms. Shealy said over lunch in Lexington, wearing an “America 250” necklace just like one she planned to give to Ms. Graham. “She didn’t go down to Mar-a-Lago or play golf.”

Ms. Shealy has been frustrated by online chatter suggesting that Ms. Graham would blindly follow the president. She described her friend as more principled than partisan.

“Lindsey and Trump weren’t always friends — they disagreed,” Ms. Shealy said. “I see Darline that way too.”

On Sunday, two days after Mr. Trump’s endorsement, Ms. Shealy texted her friend.

She knew the president supported Ms. Graham, but she wanted to make sure she had the backing of someone closer to home.

“You have always listened first, cared deeply about people, and treated everyone with dignity, regardless of whether they agreed with you,” Ms. Shealy wrote in a text reviewed by The New York Times. “South Carolina could use more of that.”

Ms. Graham replied.

“This message from you could not have come at a better time,” she wrote. “I have been praying hard. You are so right, I loved Lindsey beyond words and if I do decide to run it will not be for self ambition it will be to carry on Lindsey’s legacy and to help the people of SC.”

The next day, she announced that she would compete for her brother’s seat.

item.title: Good Samaritan in Arkansas Rides to the Rescue in a Spider-Man Costume
item.description:
Christopher Hellenthal could have changed out of his Spider-Man costume before leaving work on Tuesday. It was high noon and over 100 degrees in his Arkansas town.

Instead, he kept the costume on, mask and all, for the short drive home from his job at a trampoline park in Jonesboro.

“It’s skintight, but it’s breathable,” he said in a phone interview.

As Mr. Hellenthal, 20, stopped his red truck at a multilane intersection, he saw a man in a wheelchair struggling to cross the street at a red light. Mr. Hellenthal put the truck in park and jumped out to push the wheelchair to the other side. Then he sprinted back and drove away when the light turned green.

The interaction lasted less than a minute, but a traffic camera caught it on video and the Jonesboro Police Department posted the footage on social media hours later.

“Some people say cops are heroes, but even we need a little helping hand,” the department said in an accompanying post. “Earlier today, a citizen needing a little assistance got it in the form of a true superhero.”

On the internet, residents of Jonesboro and beyond applauded Mr. Hellenthal’s actions and marveled at his speed. Some wondered if the incident was a deleted scene from “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” a movie that arrives in theaters next week.

Others asked if the episode might have been staged to promote the film — a suggestion that Mr. Hellenthal denied in an interview on Thursday. Neither Marvel nor Sony Pictures, the film’s distributor, responded to requests for comment.

Mr. Hellenthal said he did not know the man he had assisted. “I told him, ‘Don’t worry, I’ve got you,’” he said. “It happened really fast. I just kind of skedaddled out of there because the light turned green.”

It wasn’t the first Spider-Man sighting in Jonesboro, a long way from the Marvel character’s home in New York City.

Mr. Hellenthal said he had worn the red-and-blue suit around town a few times after buying it for $200 this year from an online costume store. Once, he picked up pizza at Little Caesar’s, which was offering a special “webberoni” pie to promote the web-slinging superhero’s new movie.

“I’d call and say, ‘My name’s Peter, I need to order a webberoni,’ and I’d show up there in the costume,” Mr. Hellenthal said, referring to Spider-Man’s alter ego, Peter Parker.

Mr. Hellenthal said he had worked at Ultimate Air Trampoline Park in Jonesboro for three years, mostly during his summer breaks from college at Arkansas State University. On Tuesday, the park hosted a superhero-themed event for children.

“I wanted a suit that would look real to them,” Mr. Hellenthal said.

Much like Peter Parker, Mr. Hellenthal said, he had an interest in the sciences. The character developed spidey senses after being bitten by a radioactive spider in a laboratory; the Arkansas iteration has been working toward a bachelor’s degree in wildlife.

“He’s always been my favorite superhero,” Mr. Hellenthal said. “He’s got problems like regular people. He’s not rich, and he’s real humble, not like Tony Stark,” he added, referring to the billionaire businessman behind Iron Man.

When he was 8, Mr. Hellenthal said, he wore a Spider-Man costume when his parents brought him to a Comic Con convention in Chicago to meet Stan Lee, the character’s creator.

Mr. Hellenthal’s father, Chason Hellenthal, a beekeeper, said by phone that his youngest son had been doing good deeds his whole life.

“It just so happened this got caught on camera,” he said.
